ABSTRACT Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) with different acidity and alkalinity were applied for biomass pretreatment, and the conditions were optimized by response surface methodology. The results showed that lactic acid/betaine hydrochloride had the optimal pretreatment efficiency, where the removal rates of hemicellulose and lignin came up to 89% and 73%, and the enzymolysis efficiency was as high as 92%. Furthermore, eight types of chloride salts with different valence states were introduced into the DESs as the third component. The chloride salts could improve the pretreatment efficiency and positively correlated with the metal valence state. Specifically, AlCl3 was significantly superior in improving the pretreatment efficiency, where the enzymolysis efficiency reached 96% due to the destruction of crystalline region and the esterification of partial cellulose. Therefore, it is proposed that adding highly valent metal salts to acidic DESs has higher pretreatment and enzymatic efficiency.

1. Introduction The depletion of unrenewable resources and the conjuncture of ecological circumstances lead to an increasing interest in lignocellulosic biomass as a green, renewable, and sustainable resource (Yiin et al., 2021). However, the compact structure and complex chemical composition of the lignocellulosic biomass greatly hinder its high-valued utilization. (Ma et al., 2015). Therefore, pretreatment is essential to improve lignocellulosic biomass utilization by disrupting the physico-chemical structure and selectively separating components (Mankar et al., 2021a).

Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been regarded as effective green solvents that can effectively dissolve and separate the components of lignocellulosic biomass. Abbott and his colleagues defined the DESs as low-melting-temperature mixtures, and they synthesize a transparent solution using choline chloride and urea at low temperatures. (Abbott et al., 2004). Compared with Ionic Liquids, DESs have the advantages of easy preparation, low price, less toxic, green and easy recycling, etc., which makes it useful in many fields (Carriazo et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018). Currently, the acidic DESs are primarily investigated, mainly consisting of organic acids such as lactic acid, malonic acid, and citric acid as hydrogen-bond donors (HBD), combined with the hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA). The acidic DESs are suitable for the pretreatment of various lignocellulosic materials. When the walnut, peach endocarp and coconut are pretreated with the DES composed of lactic acid/choline chloride, the delignification rate can reach 66.3%, 70.2% and 82%, respectively, with the purity above 90% (Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Mankar et al., 2021b). In addition to acid-based DESs, alcohol-based DESs have also been concerned. Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2016) pretreated corn cobs using ethylene glycol/ChCl and glycerol/ChCl at the same molar ratio condition (2:1), and delignification rates were up to 87.6% and 71.3%, respectively. Further studies have found that the separation efficiency of the lignocellulosic biomass drastically increased by adding a third component into the binary DESs. (Lee et al., 2009; Xia et al., 2018). Generally, the third component has the following effects: reducing the viscosity of the DESs (Kandanelli et al.,

2018; Kumar et al., 2016), enhancing the lignin solubility in the DESs system, and providing active protons and acidic sites (Chen et al., 2018). According to the previous research, metal chlorides can selectively catalyze the hemicellulose degradation from lignocellulosic biomass, exhibiting diverse effects with different valence states of the metal cations (Kamireddy et al., 2013). Based on the above analysis, metal cations are introduced into the DESs to increase the acidic sites and promote the separation efficiency of the lignocellulosic biomass.

In the present work, the representative acid (lactic acid) and alcohol (glycerol) are utilized as the HBD to combine with four types of HBA for DESs preparation. Then the DES with the best separation effect is opti- mized and investigated in the pretreatment of eucalyptus wood chips by response surface methodology. Furthermore, metal chloride salts with different valence states are added into the DESs, and the variation of the H-bond ability was analyzed by observing the polarity parameters. The purpose of this research is to clarify the mechanism of the selective ac- tion of binary and ternary DESs on the lignocellulosic biomass and establish a theoretical basis for the efficient and environment-friendly conversion of lignocellulosic biomass.

2.5. Preparation and pretreatment of three-constituent deep eutectic solvents Lactic acid, betaine hydrochloride and metal chloride salts including FeCl3·6H2O, AlCl3, CuCl2·2H2O, KCl, NaCl, MgCl2, NH4Cl and ZnCl2 were mixed at 80 °C with a certain molar ratio to prepare the three-constituent deep eutectic solvent (3c-DESs), marked as DESs/FeCl3, DESs/AlCl3, DESs/CuCl2, DESs/ZnCl2, DESs/MgCl2, DESs/NaCl, DESs/NH4Cl, and DESs/KCl, respectively. The eucalyptus wood powders and 3c-DESs were mixed and reacted at 90–130 °C for 30–120 min, with a fixed mass ratio of 1:10. After reaction, the solid residues were sequentially washed using ethanol/water and deionized water, and the conditions were as the same as the above (Xia et al., 2018).

## 2.6. Determination of Kamlet-Taft parameters The determination of Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters has been described in detail in previous research (Xia et al., 2018), where N, N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline is applied as the indicator for π*, Nile red dye and 4-nitroaniline are the indicators for α and β, respectively.

## 2.7. Enzymolysis process Enzymatic hydrolysis was performed in duplicate according to the Laboratory Analytical Procedure of NREL ([Kim et al., 2019](https://example.com)). 1 g of the solid residues were added into the buffer solution composed of acetic acid and sodium acetate (pH 4.8, 0.1 mol/L), then added 30 FPU/g cellulase, 37.25 CBU/g cellobiase and three drops of ethyl acetate. The above mixture was placed into a shaker at 50 °C for 72 h, with a rotational speed of 150 rpm.

## 2.8. Characterization of the raw material and solid residues The hemicellulose, cellulose and lignin contents in the solid residues were determined by the NREL LAB method, where a two-step hydrolysis using H2SO4 was conducted (Kim et al., 2019). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, Agilent 2000) equipped with a Bio-Rad Aminex HPX-87H (300×7.8 mm) column was used to determine the sugars contents, and the determination conditions were as follows: column temperature 45 °C, mobile phase H2SO4 (0.005 mol/L) with a flow rate of 0.6 mL/min; injection volume 10 µL, and RID detector. The acid-soluble lignin in the hydrolysis solution was determined by spectrophotometry at 205 nm, and the unhydrolyzed part was used to measure the acid-insoluble lignin. Sugars and by-products in pretreatment liquors were also analyzed by HPLC after the removal of undissolved cellulose solids and dissolved lignin fractions.

The raw material and the solid residues from the DESs pretreatment were characterized by Fourier transform infrared (FTIR, Tensor II, Bruckner, Germany). ### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Determination of Kamlet-Taft parameters

The polarity of DESs can be quantified by the Kamlet-Taft parameters, where α, β and π* represented the H-bond providing capacity, H-bond accepting capacity and polarity/polarizability, respectively. The α and β were critical for the pretreatment efficiency, where a higher α value indicated that more H+ would be released, while the higher β value represented more H-bonds would be formed (Florindo et al., 2018). Therefore, the pretreatment efficiency of DESs could be inferred in advance by quantifying the difficulty of H-bond formation. It was indicated in Table 1 that the α value of lactic acid-based DESs was higher than that of glycerol-based DESs. Fig. 1a illustrated that the removal efficiency of the lignin and hemicellulose in the pretreatment using lactate-based DESs was much higher than that of glycerol-based DESs, which was confirmed by the previous research (Florindo et al., 2018), mainly because that lactic acid contained more carboxylic acid groups, which had a more substantial H-bond capacity to break the weaker H-bond connecting the glycosidic bonds in hemicellulose, and the β-O-4 bonds in lignin. On the other hand, the pKa value of HBD in DESs might also play an essential role in delignification. Apparently, the lactic acid-based DESs with higher acidity was more suitable for the delignification, which also confirmed by Mankar et al. (Mankar et al., 2021b), indicating that the highly acidic HBD could improve the dissolution of the acid-soluble lignin in DESs.

It was evident from Table 1 that the DESs consisting of lactic acid and betaine hydrochloride (1–3) had higher values of the α (2.09) and β (0.65), which was because the betaine hydrochloride contained not only chloride and nitrogen ions but also carboxylic acid groups, making it had strong electron accepting and donating capacities (Pandey et al., 2014). Factually, the DESs 1–3 indeed had the best pretreatment efficiency, as shown in Fig. 1a. Therefore, the Kamlet-Taft parameter of DESs could be applied to estimate its pretreatment effect on lignocellulose.
3.2. Effects of the pretreatment on lignocellulose separation and enzymolysis

As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the glycerol-based DESs had a poor effect on removing hemicellulose and lignin from lignocellulose, similar to the results of Hou et al. (2018). The more hydroxyl groups in glycerol increased the viscosity of DESs and thus negatively affected the dissolution of lignin and hemicellulose (Xia et al., 2018).

In addition, the carboxylic acid group in lactic acid could provide more protons to crack the glycoside, ester, and ether bonds than that of the hydroxyl group in glycerol, resulting in better solubility of hemicellulose as well as lignin. Notably, the DESs 1-3 had the best pretreatment efficiency, where cellulose retention, hemicellulose and lignin removal were 96%, 89%, and 74%, respectively, which might be because the active proton (Cl) in HBA could compete with the carbohydrates and lignin to form H-bond, also could break the ether bond in LCC (Lignin-Carbohydrate Complex) (Chen et al., 2022).

In addition, the carboxyl group in betaine hydrochloride could also form strong H-bond interactions. As shown in Table 4, the content of the by-products, such as formic acid, acetic acid, and furfural, was at a very low level, and the 5-HMF was not found in the pretreatment liquor. Compared to the glyceryl-DESs, the lactic acid-based DESs could accel- erate the furfural generation, as verified by Lee et al. (2019). It demonstrated that the acidic carboxylic group in DESs significantly cracked the β-1,4 glycosidic bonds.

In accordance with the pretreatment results, the enzymatic efficiency of the samples that pretreated using DESs 1–3 was also at the highest level (92%), as shown in Fig. 1b. The enzymatic efficiency was positively correlated with the degradation of lignin and hemicellulose, which could expose more contact points between the cellulose and cellulase (Yu et al., 2016). Interestingly, though the pretreatment efficiency of the DESs 2–3 was not excellent, the enzymatic efficiency was still as high as 89%, indicating that the alkaline co-solvent could easily swell the fibrillar structure and reduce the interaction of the H-bond network. Furthermore, the cationization of glycerol and cellulose by betaine hy-drochloride could enhance fibrillar swelling (Hong et al., 2020). At the same time, the hemicellulose removal of the sample pretreated using DESS 2–3 was obviously higher than that of other glycerol-DESs due to the action of betaine hydrochloride chloride ion.

3.4. Polarity analysis of three-constituent deep eutectic solvent For further improving the pretreatment efficiency and reducing the energy consumption, metal chloride salts were introduced into the two-consistent DESs, which could provide more acidic sites and had Lewis acid effects on the raw material pretreatment. Hence, eight types of the chloride salts containing KCl, NaCl, NHCl, MgCl2, ZnCl2, CuCl2, AlCl3 and FeCl3 were utilized as the third components of the DESs to pretreat the lignocellulosic biomass.

The influence of the metal chloride salts on the DESs was determined by the Kamlet-Taft parameters. In Table 3, all of the 3c-DESs had higher α values, indicating that the 3c-DESs could easily donate H-bonds and had high acidity. In particular, the promotion effect of metal chloride on the α value for glycerol-based DESs was greater than that of lactic acid-based DESs. The α value was elevated from 0.77 to 1.99 with the AlCl₃ added to glycerol/choline chloride, which might be due to the metal chloride salts provided a large number of active protons could not only weaken the internal H-bond in glycerol, but also added more acidic sites. The H-bond sites had been sufficient enough in the lactic acid/betaine hydrochloride and challenging to form more acidic sites even added metal chloride salts, so the α value changed slightly. However, the β value fluctuated with the addition of metal salts, which was probably corresponded to the formation of Lewis acid that weakened the H-bond receptor. For the π* value, it was did not changed with the addition of metal salts. Overall, the metal chloride salts added into the acidic DESs could also provide Lewis-acid effects in addition to the strong H-bond.
3.5. Effects of the three-constituent deep eutectic solvent on the pretreatment and enzymolysis efficiency

After adding metal chloride salts with different valence in DESs, the contents of hemicellulose and lignin in solid residues were further decreased, significantly varying with the types of metal ions in the chloride salts, as shown in In Fig. 3(a). The trivalent metal ion had a positive influence on the degradation of hemicellulose and lignin, while this influence was obviously weakened for the monovalent metal ion, indicating that the reduction of these two components was in direct proportion to the valence state of the metal ions. The addition of the metal chloride salts could provide the active protons (Cl-) for the DESs, which competed with betaine hydrochloride and formed stronger H-

Therefore, the metal chloride salts with high valence state had better H-bond donor ability, which could be illustrated by their a value changes (Table 3). At the same time, because of the three-electron redox properties of the AlCl3, electron-rich oxygen could be attracted to form a polyhedral co- ordination cage centered on the Al3+, and the formation of specific H- bonds with lactic acid further enhanced the proton transfer ability of the lactic acid, which promoted the destruction of the H-bond network of the lignocellulosic biomass. In the Fig. 3(b) concerning on the compo- nents variation, the pretreatment using DESs/AlCl3 had the best selec- tive fractionation efficiency, where the removal rates of the hemicellulose and lignin were as high as 95% and 86%, respectively.

In accordance with the pretreatment efficiency, the generation of by-products was also positively correlated with the valence state of the metal ions. When the 3c-DESs were used in the pretreatment instead of the two-constituent DESs, the concentration of all the by-products was increased (Table 5), meaning that the removal rates of hemicellulose and lignin were promoted by the Lewis acidic effects of the metal chloride salts. However, the further degradation of monosaccharides was also intensified that the contents of FF, 5-HMF, small molecular acids etc. were distinctly raised, which was not conducive to the DESs recycling the high-value utilization of sugars in the pretreatment solu-tion (Chen et al., 2022).

It was clearly shown in Fig. 3(a) that the enzymolysis efficiency was significantly improved by pretreatment using DESs, which was further enhanced by the metal chloride salts in the DESs, with a positive relationship to the valence state of the metal ions. Along with the hemicellulose and lignin degradation in the pretreatment, more attachment sites between the cellulose and cellulase were exposed, improving the enzymolysis efficiency. Therefore, the highest enzymolysis efficiency was emerged in the pretreatment using DESs-AlCl3, as high as 96%.

3.6. Molecular structure changes for the raw material and solid residues In the Fig. 4(a), the XRD results showed that typical diffraction peaks associated with cellulose I (2θ = 14.5°, 16.5° and 22.5°) were found in the raw material and all of the pretreated solid residues, indicating that the pretreated cellulose still retained its original structure. Comparing to the raw material, the CrI of the pretreated solid residues was obviously increased. In particular, the CrI of the solid residues from the pretreatment using DESs-AlCl3 was raised about 9%, this value was clearly lower than that of using the other 3c-DESs (about 18%). Compared with other

metal chloride salts, the AlCl3 could provide more active sites (Cl¯), and the Al3+ with high activity could form polyhedral coordination species to enhance the ability of donor H-bond. As a result, the glycosidic bonds in the crystalline region of cellulose were also destroyed. Thus, the CrI of the solid residues was increased at a low level (Liu et al., 2016).

The molecular changes of the raw material in the pretreatment are illustrated in Fig. 4(b), and the assignment of the absorption peaks has been reported in detail in the references (Sai and Lee, 2019). The typical absorption peaks at 1594, 1504, 1461 and 1423 cm⁻¹ were assigned to the aromatic ring in lignin, their signal intensity was obviously weak- ened after the pretreatment using DESs and 3c-DESs. The peaks at 1594 and 1504 cm⁻¹ were the skeleton vibrations of the aromatic ring, where the peak at 1461 cm⁻¹ was the signal of C-H asymmetric deformation, and the peak for the C-H deformation in the plane of the skeleton vi- brations of the aromatic ring was found at 1423 cm⁻¹. The most varia- tion of the molecular structural for the solid residues was emerged in the pretreatment using DESs/AlCl₃, DESs/FeCl₃, and DESs/CuCl₂, indi- cating that the delignification effect of metal ions with high valence state was more efficient.

The absorption peaks concerning on the cellulose were emerged at 1373, 1326, 1162, 1040 and 898 cm⁻¹, where 1373, 1326 and 898 cm⁻¹ represented the characteristic peaks of type I cellulose, and no signal changes was found after the pretreatment using 3c-DESs, this result was in accordance with the XRD analysis. The characteristic absorption peaks at 1040 and 898 cm⁻¹ represented the glycosidic bonds of cellulose, and the signal intensity was not improved with the pretreatment using 3c-DESs, namely the cellulosic glycoside bond was very stable (Ha et al., 2011). In addition, the peak at 1735 cm⁻¹ was assigned to the C = O stretching vibration, the enhancement of the signal corresponding to the esterification reaction between the hydroxyl groups in cellulose and the lactic acid, which enhanced the repulsive force among the fibers and formed a stable, negatively charged suspension (Fig. 4(b)).

3.7. Microstructure characterization of the raw material and solid residues Microstructural changes of the raw material during the pretreatment are plotted (see supplementary material). It was evident that most of the fiber bundles of the raw material were tightly combined and wrapped by rough lamellar structures (see supplementary material), which hindered the accessibility of the cellulase to cellulose. After pretreatment, the connection among the single-fiber or fiber bundle was loosed, producing more cracks and pores. In particular, the fibrous bundle from the pretreatment using DESs/AlCl3 (see supplementary material) was seriously damaged, with a transverse fracture on the cross-sectional surface. Ultimately, the perimeter protection "barriers" for the cellulose was removed, along with a small proportion of the cellulose dissolved.

## 4. Conclusions The lactic acid-based DESs with high polarity had significant efficiency for the pretreatment and enzymolysis. The carboxyl group, Cl- and N+ could promote the breakage of glycosidic-, ether- and hydrogen-bonds. The cellulose was partially esterified and improved the enzymolysis. The DESs combined with trivalent metal chlorides had abundant active sites and further depolymerized the hemicellulose and lignin, which formed porous microstructures in solid residues. The DESs-AlCl3 had the best pretreatment efficiency, where the removal rates of lignin and hemicellulose, and enzymolysis efficiency were 86%, 95% and 96%, respectively. It provided a new perspective for efficiently separating lignocellulose from green solvents.

Introduction The depletion of unrenewable resources and the conjuncture of ecological circumstances lead to an increasing interest in lignocellulosic biomass as a green, renewable, and sustainable resource (Yiin et al., 2021). However, the compact structure and complex chemical composition of the lignocellulosic biomass greatly hinder its high-valued utilization. (Ma et al., 2015). Therefore, pretreatment is essential to improve lignocellulosic biomass utilization by disrupting the physico-chemical structure and selectively separating components (Mankar et al., 2021a). Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been regarded as effective green solvents that can effectively dissolve and separate the components of lignocellulosic biomass. Abbott and his colleagues defined the DESs as low-melting-temperature mixtures, and they synthesize a transparent solution using choline chloride and urea at low temperatures. (Abbott et al., 2004). Compared with Ionic Liquids, DESs have the advantages of easy preparation, low price, less toxic, green and easy recycling, etc., which makes it useful in many fields (Carriazo et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018). Currently, the acidic DESs are primarily investigated, mainly consisting of organic acids such as lactic acid, malonic acid, and citric acid as hydrogen-bond donors (HBD), combined with the hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA). The acidic DESs are suitable for the pretreatment of various lignocellulosic materials. When the walnut, peach endocarp and coconut are pretreated with the DES composed of lactic acid/choline chloride, the delignification rate can reach 66.3%, 70.2% and 82%, respectively, with the purity above 90% (Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Mankar et al., 2021b). In addition to acid-based DESs, alcohol-based DESs have also been concerned. Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2016) pretreated corn cobs using ethylene glycol/ChCl and glycerol/ChCl at the same molar ratio condition (2:1), and delignification rates were up to 87.6% and 71.3%, respectively. Further studies have found that the separation efficiency of the lignocellulosic biomass drastically increased by adding a third component into the binary DESs. (Lee et al., 2009; Xia et al., 2018). Generally, the third component has the following effects: reducing the viscosity of the DESs (Kandanelli et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2016), enhancing the lignin solubility in the DESs system, and providing active protons and acidic sites (Chen et al., 2018). According to the previous research, metal chlorides can selectively catalyze the hemicellulose degradation from lignocellulosic biomass, exhibiting diverse effects with different valence states of the metal cations (Kamireddy et al., 2013). Based on the above analysis, metal cations are introduced into the DESs to increase the acidic sites and promote the separation efficiency of the lignocellulosic biomass. In the present work, the representative acid (lactic acid) and alcohol (glycerol) are utilized as the HBD to combine with four types of HBA for DESs preparation. Then the DES with the best separation effect is opti- mized and investigated in the pretreatment of eucalyptus wood chips by response surface methodology. Furthermore, metal chloride salts with different valence states are added into the DESs, and the variation of the H-bond ability was analyzed by observing the polarity parameters. The purpose of this research is to clarify the mechanism of the selective ac- tion of binary and ternary DESs on the lignocellulosic biomass and establish a theoretical basis for the efficient and environment-friendly conversion of lignocellulosic biomass. ## 2. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Determination of Kamlet-Taft parameters The polarity of DESs can be quantified by the Kamlet-Taft parameters, where α, β and π* represented the H-bond providing capacity, H-bond accepting capacity and polarity/polarizability, respectively. The α and β were critical for the pretreatment efficiency, where a higher α value indicated that more H+ would be released, while the higher β value represented more H-bonds would be formed (Florindo et al., 2018). Therefore, the pretreatment efficiency of DESs could be inferred in advance by quantifying the difficulty of H-bond formation. It was indicated in Table 1 that the α value of lactic acid-based DESs was higher than that of glycerol-based DESs. Fig. 1a illustrated that the removal efficiency of the lignin and hemicellulose in the pretreatment using lactate-based DESs was much higher than that of glycerol-based DESs, which was confirmed by the previous research (Florindo et al., 2018), mainly because that lactic acid contained more carboxylic acid groups, which had a more substantial H-bond capacity to break the weaker H-bond connecting the glycosidic bonds in hemicellulose, and the β-O-4 bonds in lignin. On the other hand, the pKa value of HBD in DESs might also play an essential role in delignification. Apparently, the lactic acid-based DESs with higher acidity was more suitable for the delignification, which also confirmed by Mankar et al. (Mankar et al., 2021b), indicating that the highly acidic HBD could improve the dissolution of the acid-soluble lignin in DESs. It was evident from Table 1 that the DESs consisting of lactic acid and betaine hydrochloride (1–3) had higher values of the α (2.09) and β (0.65), which was because the betaine hydrochloride contained not only chloride and nitrogen ions but also carboxylic acid groups, making it had strong electron accepting and donating capacities (Pandey et al., 2014). Factually, the DESs 1–3 indeed had the best pretreatment efficiency, as shown in Fig. 1a. Therefore, the Kamlet-Taft parameter of DESs could be applied to estimate its pretreatment effect on lignocellulose. 3.2. Effects of the pretreatment on lignocellulose separation and enzymolysis As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the glycerol-based DESs had a poor effect on removing hemicellulose and lignin from lignocellulose, similar to the results of Hou et al. (2018). The more hydroxyl groups in glycerol increased the viscosity of DESs and thus negatively affected the dissolution of lignin and hemicellulose (Xia et al., 2018). In addition, the carboxylic acid group in lactic acid could provide more protons to crack the glycoside, ester, and ether bonds than that of the hydroxyl group in glycerol, resulting in better solubility of hemicellulose as well as lignin. Notably, the DESs 1-3 had the best pretreatment efficiency, where cellulose retention, hemicellulose and lignin removal were 96%, 89%, and 74%, respectively, which might be because the active proton (Cl) in HBA could compete with the carbohydrates and lignin to form H-bond, also could break the ether bond in LCC (Lignin-Carbohydrate Complex) (Chen et al., 2022). In addition, the carboxyl group in betaine hydrochloride could also form strong H-bond interactions. As shown in Table 4, the content of the by-products, such as formic acid, acetic acid, and furfural, was at a very low level, and the 5-HMF was not found in the pretreatment liquor. Compared to the glyceryl-DESs, the lactic acid-based DESs could accel- erate the furfural generation, as verified by Lee et al. (2019). It demonstrated that the acidic carboxylic group in DESs significantly cracked the β-1,4 glycosidic bonds. In accordance with the pretreatment results, the enzymatic efficiency of the samples that pretreated using DESs 1–3 was also at the highest level (92%), as shown in Fig. 1b. The enzymatic efficiency was positively correlated with the degradation of lignin and hemicellulose, which could expose more contact points between the cellulose and cellulase (Yu et al., 2016). Interestingly, though the pretreatment efficiency of the DESs 2–3 was not excellent, the enzymatic efficiency was still as high as 89%, indicating that the alkaline co-solvent could easily swell the fibrillar structure and reduce the interaction of the H-bond network. Furthermore, the cationization of glycerol and cellulose by betaine hy-drochloride could enhance fibrillar swelling (Hong et al., 2020). At the same time, the hemicellulose removal of the sample pretreated using DESS 2–3 was obviously higher than that of other glycerol-DESs due to the action of betaine hydrochloride chloride ion. 3.3. In particular, the CrI of the solid residues from the pretreatment using DESs-AlCl3 was raised about 9%, this value was clearly lower than that of using the other 3c-DESs (about 18%). Compared with other metal chloride salts, the AlCl3 could provide more active sites (Cl¯), and the Al3+ with high activity could form polyhedral coordination species to enhance the ability of donor H-bond. As a result, the glycosidic bonds in the crystalline region of cellulose were also destroyed. Thus, the CrI of the solid residues was increased at a low level (Liu et al., 2016). The molecular changes of the raw material in the pretreatment are illustrated in Fig. 4(b), and the assignment of the absorption peaks has been reported in detail in the references (Sai and Lee, 2019). The typical absorption peaks at 1594, 1504, 1461 and 1423 cm⁻¹ were assigned to the aromatic ring in lignin, their signal intensity was obviously weak- ened after the pretreatment using DESs and 3c-DESs. The peaks at 1594 and 1504 cm⁻¹ were the skeleton vibrations of the aromatic ring, where the peak at 1461 cm⁻¹ was the signal of C-H asymmetric deformation, and the peak for the C-H deformation in the plane of the skeleton vi- brations of the aromatic ring was found at 1423 cm⁻¹. The most varia- tion of the molecular structural for the solid residues was emerged in the pretreatment using DESs/AlCl₃, DESs/FeCl₃, and DESs/CuCl₂, indi- cating that the delignification effect of metal ions with high valence state was more efficient. The absorption peaks concerning on the cellulose were emerged at 1373, 1326, 1162, 1040 and 898 cm⁻¹, where 1373, 1326 and 898 cm⁻¹ represented the characteristic peaks of type I cellulose, and no signal changes was found after the pretreatment using 3c-DESs, this result was in accordance with the XRD analysis. The characteristic absorption peaks at 1040 and 898 cm⁻¹ represented the glycosidic bonds of cellulose, and the signal intensity was not improved with the pretreatment using 3c-DESs, namely the cellulosic glycoside bond was very stable (Ha et al., 2011). In addition, the peak at 1735 cm⁻¹ was assigned to the C = O stretching vibration, the enhancement of the signal corresponding to the esterification reaction between the hydroxyl groups in cellulose and the lactic acid, which enhanced the repulsive force among the fibers and formed a stable, negatively charged suspension (Fig. 4(b)). 3.7. Microstructure characterization of the raw material and solid residues Microstructural changes of the raw material during the pretreatment are plotted (see supplementary material). It was evident that most of the fiber bundles of the raw material were tightly combined and wrapped by rough lamellar structures (see supplementary material), which hindered the accessibility of the cellulase to cellulose. After pretreatment, the connection among the single-fiber or fiber bundle was loosed, producing more cracks and pores. In particular, the fibrous bundle from the pretreatment using DESs/AlCl3 (see supplementary material) was seriously damaged, with a transverse fracture on the cross-sectional surface. Ultimately, the perimeter protection "barriers" for the cellulose was removed, along with a small proportion of the cellulose dissolved. ## 4. Conclusions The lactic acid-based DESs with high polarity had significant efficiency for the pretreatment and enzymolysis. The carboxyl group, Cl- and N+ could promote the breakage of glycosidic-, ether- and hydrogen-bonds. The cellulose was partially esterified and improved the enzymolysis. The DESs combined with trivalent metal chlorides had abundant active sites and further depolymerized the hemicellulose and lignin, which formed porous microstructures in solid residues. The DESs-AlCl3 had the best pretreatment efficiency, where the removal rates of lignin and hemicellulose, and enzymolysis efficiency were 86%, 95% and 96%, respectively. It provided a new perspective for efficiently separating lignocellulose from green solvents. Introduction The depletion of unrenewable resources and the conjuncture of ecological circumstances lead to an increasing interest in lignocellulosic biomass as a green, renewable, and sustainable resource (Yiin et al., 2021). However, the compact structure and complex chemical composition of the lignocellulosic biomass greatly hinder its high-valued utilization. (Ma et al., 2015). Therefore, pretreatment is essential to improve lignocellulosic biomass utilization by disrupting the physico-chemical structure and selectively separating components (Mankar et al., 2021a). Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been regarded as effective green solvents that can effectively dissolve and separate the components of lignocellulosic biomass. Abbott and his colleagues defined the DESs as low-melting-temperature mixtures, and they synthesize a transparent solution using choline chloride and urea at low temperatures. (Abbott et al., 2004). Compared with Ionic Liquids, DESs have the advantages of easy preparation, low price, less toxic, green and easy recycling, etc., which makes it useful in many fields (Carriazo et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018). Currently, the acidic DESs are primarily investigated, mainly consisting of organic acids such as lactic acid, malonic acid, and citric acid as hydrogen-bond donors (HBD), combined with the hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA). The acidic DESs are suitable for the pretreatment of various lignocellulosic materials. When the walnut, peach endocarp and coconut are pretreated with the DES composed of lactic acid/choline chloride, the delignification rate can reach 66.3%, 70.2% and 82%, respectively, with the purity above 90% (Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Mankar et al., 2021b). In addition to acid-based DESs, alcohol-based DESs have also been concerned. Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2016) pretreated corn cobs using ethylene glycol/ChCl and glycerol/ChCl at the same molar ratio condition (2:1), and delignification rates were up to 87.6% and 71.3%, respectively. Further studies have found that the separation efficiency of the lignocellulosic biomass drastically increased by adding a third component into the binary DESs. (Lee et al., 2009; Xia et al., 2018). Generally, the third component has the following effects: reducing the viscosity of the DESs (Kandanelli et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2016), enhancing the lignin solubility in the DESs system, and providing active protons and acidic sites (Chen et al., 2018). According to the previous research, metal chlorides can selectively catalyze the hemicellulose degradation from lignocellulosic biomass, exhibiting diverse effects with different valence states of the metal cations (Kamireddy et al., 2013). Based on the above analysis, metal cations are introduced into the DESs to increase the acidic sites and promote the separation efficiency of the lignocellulosic biomass. In the present work, the representative acid (lactic acid) and alcohol (glycerol) are utilized as the HBD to combine with four types of HBA for DESs preparation. Then the DES with the best separation effect is opti- mized and investigated in the pretreatment of eucalyptus wood chips by response surface methodology. Furthermore, metal chloride salts with different valence states are added into the DESs, and the variation of the H-bond ability was analyzed by observing the polarity parameters. The purpose of this research is to clarify the mechanism of the selective ac- tion of binary and ternary DESs on the lignocellulosic biomass and establish a theoretical basis for the efficient and environment-friendly conversion of lignocellulosic biomass. ## 2. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Determination of Kamlet-Taft parameters The polarity of DESs can be quantified by the Kamlet-Taft parameters, where α, β and π* represented the H-bond providing capacity, H-bond accepting capacity and polarity/polarizability, respectively. The α and β were critical for the pretreatment efficiency, where a higher α value indicated that more H+ would be released, while the higher β value represented more H-bonds would be formed (Florindo et al., 2018). Therefore, the pretreatment efficiency of DESs could be inferred in advance by quantifying the difficulty of H-bond formation. It was indicated in Table 1 that the α value of lactic acid-based DESs was higher than that of glycerol-based DESs. Fig. 1a illustrated that the removal efficiency of the lignin and hemicellulose in the pretreatment using lactate-based DESs was much higher than that of glycerol-based DESs, which was confirmed by the previous research (Florindo et al., 2018), mainly because that lactic acid contained more carboxylic acid groups, which had a more substantial H-bond capacity to break the weaker H-bond connecting the glycosidic bonds in hemicellulose, and the β-O-4 bonds in lignin. On the other hand, the pKa value of HBD in DESs might also play an essential role in delignification. Apparently, the lactic acid-based DESs with higher acidity was more suitable for the delignification, which also confirmed by Mankar et al. (Mankar et al., 2021b), indicating that the highly acidic HBD could improve the dissolution of the acid-soluble lignin in DESs. It was evident from Table 1 that the DESs consisting of lactic acid and betaine hydrochloride (1–3) had higher values of the α (2.09) and β (0.65), which was because the betaine hydrochloride contained not only chloride and nitrogen ions but also carboxylic acid groups, making it had strong electron accepting and donating capacities (Pandey et al., 2014). Factually, the DESs 1–3 indeed had the best pretreatment efficiency, as shown in Fig. 1a. Therefore, the Kamlet-Taft parameter of DESs could be applied to estimate its pretreatment effect on lignocellulose. 3.2. Effects of the pretreatment on lignocellulose separation and enzymolysis As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the glycerol-based DESs had a poor effect on removing hemicellulose and lignin from lignocellulose, similar to the results of Hou et al. (2018). The more hydroxyl groups in glycerol increased the viscosity of DESs and thus negatively affected the dissolution of lignin and hemicellulose (Xia et al., 2018). In addition, the carboxylic acid group in lactic acid could provide more protons to crack the glycoside, ester, and ether bonds than that of the hydroxyl group in glycerol, resulting in better solubility of hemicellulose as well as lignin. Notably, the DESs 1-3 had the best pretreatment efficiency, where cellulose retention, hemicellulose and lignin removal were 96%, 89%, and 74%, respectively, which might be because the active proton (Cl) in HBA could compete with the carbohydrates and lignin to form H-bond, also could break the ether bond in LCC (Lignin-Carbohydrate Complex) (Chen et al., 2022). In addition, the carboxyl group in betaine hydrochloride could also form strong H-bond interactions. As shown in Table 4, the content of the by-products, such as formic acid, acetic acid, and furfural, was at a very low level, and the 5-HMF was not found in the pretreatment liquor. Compared to the glyceryl-DESs, the lactic acid-based DESs could accel- erate the furfural generation, as verified by Lee et al. (2019). It demonstrated that the acidic carboxylic group in DESs significantly cracked the β-1,4 glycosidic bonds. In accordance with the pretreatment results, the enzymatic efficiency of the samples that pretreated using DESs 1–3 was also at the highest level (92%), as shown in Fig. 1b. The enzymatic efficiency was positively correlated with the degradation of lignin and hemicellulose, which could expose more contact points between the cellulose and cellulase (Yu et al., 2016). Interestingly, though the pretreatment efficiency of the DESs 2–3 was not excellent, the enzymatic efficiency was still as high as 89%, indicating that the alkaline co-solvent could easily swell the fibrillar structure and reduce the interaction of the H-bond network. Furthermore, the cationization of glycerol and cellulose by betaine hy-drochloride could enhance fibrillar swelling (Hong et al., 2020). At the same time, the hemicellulose removal of the sample pretreated using DESS 2–3 was obviously higher than that of other glycerol-DESs due to the action of betaine hydrochloride chloride ion. 3.3. Polarity analysis of three-constituent deep eutectic solvent For further improving the pretreatment efficiency and reducing the energy consumption, metal chloride salts were introduced into the two-consistent DESs, which could provide more acidic sites and had Lewis acid effects on the raw material pretreatment. Hence, eight types of the chloride salts containing KCl, NaCl, NHCl, MgCl2, ZnCl2, CuCl2, AlCl3 and FeCl3 were utilized as the third components of the DESs to pretreat the lignocellulosic biomass. The influence of the metal chloride salts on the DESs was determined by the Kamlet-Taft parameters. In Table 3, all of the 3c-DESs had higher α values, indicating that the 3c-DESs could easily donate H-bonds and had high acidity. The H-bond sites had been sufficient enough in the lactic acid/betaine hydrochloride and challenging to form more acidic sites even added metal chloride salts, so the α value changed slightly. However, the β value fluctuated with the addition of metal salts, which was probably corresponded to the formation of Lewis acid that weakened the H-bond receptor. For the π* value, it was did not changed with the addition of metal salts. Overall, the metal chloride salts added into the acidic DESs could also provide Lewis-acid effects in addition to the strong H-bond. 3.5. When the 3c-DESs were used in the pretreatment instead of the two-constituent DESs, the concentration of all the by-products was increased (Table 5), meaning that the removal rates of hemicellulose and lignin were promoted by the Lewis acidic effects of the metal chloride salts. However, the further degradation of monosaccharides was also intensified that the contents of FF, 5-HMF, small molecular acids etc. were distinctly raised, which was not conducive to the DESs recycling the high-value utilization of sugars in the pretreatment solu-tion (Chen et al., 2022). It was clearly shown in Fig. 3(a) that the enzymolysis efficiency was significantly improved by pretreatment using DESs, which was further enhanced by the metal chloride salts in the DESs, with a positive relationship to the valence state of the metal ions. Along with the hemicellulose and lignin degradation in the pretreatment, more attachment sites between the cellulose and cellulase were exposed, improving the enzymolysis efficiency. Therefore, the highest enzymolysis efficiency was emerged in the pretreatment using DESs-AlCl3, as high as 96%. 3.6. Molecular structure changes for the raw material and solid residues In the Fig. 4(a), the XRD results showed that typical diffraction peaks associated with cellulose I (2θ = 14.5°, 16.5° and 22.5°) were found in the raw material and all of the pretreated solid residues, indicating that the pretreated cellulose still retained its original structure. Comparing to the raw material, the CrI of the pretreated solid residues was obviously increased. In particular, the CrI of the solid residues from the pretreatment using DESs-AlCl3 was raised about 9%, this value was clearly lower than that of using the other 3c-DESs (about 18%). Compared with other metal chloride salts, the AlCl3 could provide more active sites (Cl¯), and the Al3+ with high activity could form polyhedral coordination species to enhance the ability of donor H-bond. As a result, the glycosidic bonds in the crystalline region of cellulose were also destroyed. Thus, the CrI of the solid residues was increased at a low level (Liu et al., 2016). The molecular changes of the raw material in the pretreatment are illustrated in Fig. 4(b), and the assignment of the absorption peaks has been reported in detail in the references (Sai and Lee, 2019). The typical absorption peaks at 1594, 1504, 1461 and 1423 cm⁻¹ were assigned to the aromatic ring in lignin, their signal intensity was obviously weak- ened after the pretreatment using DESs and 3c-DESs. The peaks at 1594 and 1504 cm⁻¹ were the skeleton vibrations of the aromatic ring, where the peak at 1461 cm⁻¹ was the signal of C-H asymmetric deformation, and the peak for the C-H deformation in the plane of the skeleton vi- brations of the aromatic ring was found at 1423 cm⁻¹. The most varia- tion of the molecular structural for the solid residues was emerged in the pretreatment using DESs/AlCl₃, DESs/FeCl₃, and DESs/CuCl₂, indi- cating that the delignification effect of metal ions with high valence state was more efficient. The absorption peaks concerning on the cellulose were emerged at 1373, 1326, 1162, 1040 and 898 cm⁻¹, where 1373, 1326 and 898 cm⁻¹ represented the characteristic peaks of type I cellulose, and no signal changes was found after the pretreatment using 3c-DESs, this result was in accordance with the XRD analysis. The characteristic absorption peaks at 1040 and 898 cm⁻¹ represented the glycosidic bonds of cellulose, and the signal intensity was not improved with the pretreatment using 3c-DESs, namely the cellulosic glycoside bond was very stable (Ha et al., 2011). In addition, the peak at 1735 cm⁻¹ was assigned to the C = O stretching vibration, the enhancement of the signal corresponding to the esterification reaction between the hydroxyl groups in cellulose and the lactic acid, which enhanced the repulsive force among the fibers and formed a stable, negatively charged suspension (Fig. 4(b)). 3.7. Microstructure characterization of the raw material and solid residues Microstructural changes of the raw material during the pretreatment are plotted (see supplementary material). It was evident that most of the fiber bundles of the raw material were tightly combined and wrapped by rough lamellar structures (see supplementary material), which hindered the accessibility of the cellulase to cellulose. After pretreatment, the connection among the single-fiber or fiber bundle was loosed, producing more cracks and pores. In particular, the fibrous bundle from the pretreatment using DESs/AlCl3 (see supplementary material) was seriously damaged, with a transverse fracture on the cross-sectional surface. Ultimately, the perimeter protection "barriers" for the cellulose was removed, along with a small proportion of the cellulose dissolved. ## 4. Conclusions The lactic acid-based DESs with high polarity had significant efficiency for the pretreatment and enzymolysis. The carboxyl group, Cl- and N+ could promote the breakage of glycosidic-, ether- and hydrogen-bonds. The cellulose was partially esterified and improved the enzymolysis. The DESs combined with trivalent metal chlorides had abundant active sites and further depolymerized the hemicellulose and lignin, which formed porous microstructures in solid residues. The DESs-AlCl3 had the best pretreatment efficiency, where the removal rates of lignin and hemicellulose, and enzymolysis efficiency were 86%, 95% and 96%, respectively. It provided a new perspective for efficiently separating lignocellulose from green solvents.
